At 6:17 in the morning, the kettle begins to sing.

The house is still dark. Outside, rain gathers on the windows and slides down in crooked little rivers. Somewhere in the wall, the pipes make a sound like someone clearing their throat. I stand barefoot on the cold kitchen floor and wait for the water to boil.

There is no particular reason to be awake. The day has not asked anything of me yet. No messages have arrived, no decisions need making. For a few minutes, the world is only this: the dim green clock, the kettle’s growing voice, the rain stitching the window shut.

I used to think a life would announce itself more clearly. I imagined the important moments would arrive with a kind of music behind them, or at least a clean line drawn between before and after. Instead, they mostly came disguised as Tuesdays. A phone call taken in the grocery store parking lot. A box carried up the stairs. An ordinary evening when someone said, “I’m glad you’re here,” and meant it.

The kettle clicks off.

I pour the water over the tea and watch the leaves turn slowly in the cup. They loosen, unfurl, darken the water. It seems a small miracle, though I know the explanation. The explanation doesn’t make it less beautiful.

Maybe that’s what time does. It doesn’t transform us all at once. It steepens us. It draws something out, little by little, until what was hidden begins to color everything.

I take the cup to the window. The street is empty except for a newspaper lying in a puddle. A light comes on in the house across the road. Someone else is awake. For a moment we share the morning without knowing each other—two lit windows, two small islands in the rain.

I wonder what they’re thinking. Maybe nothing. Maybe they’re late. Maybe they’re standing in a kitchen just like mine, holding a warm cup with both hands and trying to remember what they came in here for.

This is one of the things I love about being alive: how much of it happens beyond the reach of our explanations. The stranger who holds a door. The bird that lands on the fence and leaves before we decide to look. The way a familiar voice can alter the temperature of a room. We move through a world crowded with quiet offerings, most of them too small to keep, too numerous to count.

The rain softens. The sky, which had been the color of an old spoon, begins to pale at the edges. Soon there will be traffic. Someone will turn on a radio. The day will gather its demands.

But not yet.

I wrap my fingers around the cup. The tea is almost too hot. I wait, and while I wait I think of all the things I have mistaken for endings: the last page of a book, a door closing, a goodbye spoken in the careful voice people use when they are trying not to break something. Some things do end. There is no use pretending otherwise. But endings are not the only shape a life can take. A path can disappear beneath snow and still be there. A song can stop, and the note can remain in the room for a while.

The first sip is bitter, then warm.

In the next house, the light goes out. Perhaps they have left. Perhaps they have gone back to bed. I don’t know, and the not knowing is peaceful. The morning does not need me to understand every window.

Soon, I’ll put on socks. I’ll open the door. The air will smell of wet stone and leaves. I’ll step into the day carrying no great revelation—only the small warmth of the cup, the rain’s brief attention, the knowledge that somewhere, even now, other kettles are beginning to sing.
